nameStory: The grapevine beetle gets its name from its favorite food source - grape leaves and vines, which both adults and their grubs munch on throughout their life cycle. Despite this dining preference, these beetles are surprisingly gentle on their host plants, doing relatively little damage compared to other plant-eating insects. They're also called spotted June beetles for their distinctive black polka dots and their peak activity during early summer months.
description: The grapevine beetle is a chunky, colorful member of the scarab beetle family that looks like nature decorated it for a party. These inch-long beetles sport a striking pattern of creamy yellow to reddish-brown coloring with bold black spots marching down their sides like military stripes. They're fast, curvy fliers that you'll often see zooming around in erratic patterns during warm summer evenings. At about an inch long (occasionally reaching 1.2 inches), they're substantial enough to notice but small enough to land gently on your hand.

idTips.label: Spotted Pattern
idTips.description: Four distinct black spots line each side of the wing covers, creating a polka-dot pattern that's unmistakable when the beetle is at rest

idTips.label: Color Variation
idTips.description: Base color ranges from pale cream-yellow to warm auburn-red, with northern beetles typically showing darker, richer tones than their southern cousins

idTips.label: Wing Cover Edges
idTips.description: Fine black lines trace the outer edges of the hard wing covers (elytra), creating a neat border around the beetle's back

idTips.label: Size and Shape
idTips.description: Robust, oval-shaped body about the size of your thumbnail, with a solid, heavy feel if you let one crawl on your hand

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Flies in distinctive curved, swooping patterns at surprisingly fast speeds, often bumping into lights or windows on summer nights

habitat: Look for grapevine beetles around their favorite food sources - wild and cultivated grapevines, as well as Virginia creeper and other climbing vines. They're common in sunny edges of woodlands, old fields with grape tangles, backyard gardens with grape arbors, and anywhere wild grapes scramble up trees or fences. You'll often spot them on warm evenings flying around outdoor lights in suburban and rural areas throughout New England.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from soil in late spring as temperatures warm, but they're not yet at peak activity. Look for early individuals on young grape leaves.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs during June and July when adults are most active, flying around lights at night and feeding during the day. This is the best time to observe their characteristic flight patterns.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity winds down as beetles prepare for winter. Late-season individuals may still be found on grape vines before the first frost.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter in soil and leaf litter, remaining completely hidden and inactive until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Despite their name and grape-munching habits, grapevine beetles are actually beneficial garden visitors - they're such gentle feeders that grape growers rarely consider them pests, and their grubs help aerate soil by tunneling through decaying organic matter underground.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Japanese beetles, but grapevine beetles are larger, lack the metallic green sheen, and have distinct black spots instead of the Japanese beetle's more uniform coloring. Remember: "Grapes have spots, Japanese shine" - grapevine beetles have obvious black polka dots while Japanese beetles are glossy metallic.
contextualKnowledge: The grapevine beetle's scientific classification was once a taxonomic nightmare - in 1915, one overzealous scientist split this single species into 11 different species based on minor color variations, only to have later researchers realize they were all the same variable beetle. This explains why you might see such dramatic color differences between individual grapevine beetles in the same area.
compareHints: As the only member of its genus (Pelidnota) in New England, the grapevine beetle is unique among local scarabs for its spotted pattern and grape-feeding habits. Compared to other scarab beetles in the region, it's distinguished by its larger size, distinctive black spots, and preference for above-ground plant feeding rather than the dung or decaying matter that attracts most other scarabs. Its closest relatives are found in tropical regions and lack the cold tolerance that allows this species to thrive in New England.
